title: The nature and characteristics of memory

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The reason for the range of work that has been conducted into the questions of what, why, and how we remember should be apparent: memory is a key psychological process. As stated by eminent cognitive neuroscientist Michel Gazzaniga: ‘Everything in life is memory, save for the thin edge of the present’. Memory allows us to recall birthdays, holidays, and other significant events that may have taken place hours, days, or even years ago. Our memories are personal and ‘internal’, yet without memory we wouldn't be able to undertake ‘external’ acts — such as holding a conversation, recognizing our friends’ faces, remembering appointments, or even learning to walk.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The inconsistencies of memory can be illustrated by the following example. Without doubt, you have seen thousands of coins in your lifetime. But let us reflect on how well you can remember a typical coin in your pocket. Without looking at it, take a few minutes to try to draw a coin of a particular denomination from memory. Now compare your drawing with the coin itself. How accurate was your memory of the coin? For instance, was the head facing the correct way? How many of the words from the coin did you recall? Did you place these words correctly? Systematic studies were conducted into this topic in the 1970s and 1980s. Researchers found that most people actually don't have a very good memory when it comes to things they see almost constantly — like coins.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: This represents a type of memory which we tend to take for granted, but actually isn't as good as we think. Try to remember other commonplace items in your environment, such as stamps, or the details of clothes that other people in your workplace, or with whom you frequently socialize, typically wear. The key point here is that we generally remember the information that is most salient and helpful for us. For instance, we may be much better at remembering the typical size, dimensions or colour of coins than the direction of the head or the text on the coin. This is because the size, dimensions or colour may well be more relevant for us when we are using money (i.e. for the primary purpose of payment and exchange, for which money was devised). And when remembering people, we will typically be able to remember their faces and other distinguishing features that remain relatively unaltered (and are, therefore, most helpful in identifying them), rather than items which may change (such as individuals’ clothing).

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Instead of thinking of coins and clothing, it is perhaps more straightforward for most people to consider the way memory works in the case of a student who attends a lecture, and later brings to mind successfully what was taught in the lecture in the examination hall. This is the kind of ‘memory’ that most people, if not in fact everyone, will have come across during their school days. But it may be less obvious that memory may still play an effective role for students, even if they don't use specific facts and opinions from the lecture in an essay or exam, but instead use some of the information more generally in later life.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: But memory plays a role whether or not we intend to learn. In fact, comparatively little of our lives is employed attempting to ‘record’ events for later remembering, as in formal study. By contrast, most of the time we are simply getting on with our day-to-day lives. But when something especially significant does happen (which, in our evolutionary past as Homo sapiens, may well have been associated with threat or reward), then established physiological and psychological processes kick in, and we usually remember these events quite well. For example, many people have had the experience of forgetting where they left their car in a large car park. But if they have an accident and damage their car and/or the car of their neighbour in the car park, then specific ‘fight, fright or flight’ mechanisms are initiated, ensuring that they typically remember such events (and the location of their car) very well!

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There have been many different models of how memory works, going right back into classical times. For example, in ancient Greece, Plato regarded memory as being like a wax tablet, on which impressions would be made or words written, and subsequently stored, so that they could be retrieved at a later time. This distinction between encoding, storage and retrieval of memories has persisted among scientific investigators to the present day. Other philosophers in classical times likened memories to aviaries full of birds or to books in a library, underlining the difficulties of retrieving information after it had been stored — that is, catching the right bird or locating the right volume.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Contemporary theorists have come to appreciate that memory is a selective and interpretive process. In other words, there is more to memory than just the passive storage of information. Furthermore, after learning and storing new information, we can select, interpret and combine one thing with another — so as to make better use of what we learn and remember. This is likely to be one reason why chess experts find it easier to remember the position of pieces on a chess board, and why football fans find it easier to remember each of the football scores at the weekend, i.e. thanks to their extensive knowledge and the interconnections between different elements of this knowledge.
